questions.prompt: The RC low-pass filter has \(H(s)=1/(1+s\tau)\). Where is its pole?
questions.explanation:
Set the denominator to zero: \(1+s\tau=0\) ⇒ \(s=-1/\tau\). A negative real pole means a decaying exponential \(e^{-t/\tau}\) in the response. The magnitude of the pole, \(1/\tau\), is the corner (break) frequency in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
A positive pole would mean an exponentially growing response (unstable); \(s=0\) would be an integrator.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass has \(R=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). At what angular frequency \((\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s})\) is its pole?
questions.explanation:
\(H(s)=1/(1+sRC)\) has its pole at \(s=-1/(RC)=-1/(10^{3}\times 10^{-6})=-1000\). The pole frequency is \(\omega_{p}=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\ (f_{p}=159\ \mathrm{Hz})\).
Common mistake: answering in Hz (159 Hz) when asked for \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(R=4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(C=22\ \mathrm{nF}\). At what frequency is its pole (the −3 dB corner), in Hz?
questions.explanation:
The pole is at \(\omega_p=1/(RC)\), so \(f_p=1/(2\pi RC)=1/(2\pi\cdot4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\cdot22\ \mathrm{nF})=1.54\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
• \(1/(RC)=9.67\times10^3\) is the corner in rad/s; dividing by \(2\pi\) gives Hz.
• \(RC=103\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) is the time constant, not a frequency.

questions.prompt: An RC high-pass filter has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega\tau/(1+j\omega\tau)\), \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\). Which statement describes its pole and zero?
options: One zero at \(s=0\) and one pole at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
One zero at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and one pole at \(s=0\)
One zero at \(s=0\) and one pole at \(s=+1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
No zero, and one pole at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
questions.explanation:
With \(s=j\omega\): \(H(s)=s\tau/(1+s\tau)\). The numerator vanishes at \(s=0\) (a zero at the origin: no DC transmission). The denominator vanishes at \(s=-1/\tau=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (a pole in the left half-plane).
• Swapping the two reverses the high-pass into something like an integrator.
• A positive pole would mean an unstable (growing) response.
• The numerator is not a constant, so there is a zero.

questions.prompt: An RC high-pass filter (series \(C=0.1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), \(R=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) to ground) passes a 100 Hz tone. What is \(|V_{out}/V_{in}|\) in dB?
questions.explanation:
\(H=\dfrac{j\omega RC}{1+j\omega RC}\) with \(\omega RC=2\pi(100)(1\ \mathrm{ms})=0.628\). \(|H|=0.628/\sqrt{1+0.395}=0.532=-5.5\ \mathrm{dB}\). The tone sits below the 159 Hz corner, on the +20 dB/decade slope.
• 0 dB treats the tone as if it were in the passband.
• \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) is the value at the corner, 159 Hz.
• \(20\log_{10}0.628=-4.0\ \mathrm{dB}\) is the asymptote, which ignores the pole's rounding.

questions.prompt: An amplifier has a coupling capacitor at its input (giving a zero at DC and a pole at 20 Hz) and a load capacitance at its output (a pole at 2 MHz). Its midband gain is 26 dB. What does its Bode magnitude plot look like?
options: Flat at 26 dB from DC to 2 MHz, then falling
Rising at +20 dB/decade up to 20 Hz, flat at 26 dB from 20 Hz to 2 MHz, then falling at −20 dB/decade
Rising at +20 dB/decade up to 2 MHz, then flat
Falling from DC, with a notch at 20 Hz
questions.explanation:
The zero at the origin gives a +20 dB/decade slope from the lowest frequencies. The 20 Hz pole cancels that slope, so the gain is flat (midband) up to the 2 MHz pole, where it starts falling. This band-pass shape is typical of AC-coupled amplifiers.
• 'Flat from DC' would need DC coupling, but the capacitor blocks DC.
• The pole pairing in the third option is reversed.
• A notch would need complex zeros near 20 Hz.
questions.figure_alt: Band-pass Bode magnitude: rising at low frequency, flat midband, falling at high frequency.

questions.prompt: A circuit contains two capacitors and three resistors (and a voltage source). Which statement about the number of poles of its transfer function is correct?
options: There are 5 poles, one for each element
There are no poles unless an inductor is present
There are at most 2 poles, and fewer if the capacitors are not independent (e.g., two capacitors in parallel behave as one)
questions.explanation:
The number of poles equals the number of independent energy-storage elements (the order of the circuit's differential equation) (reader Sec. 2.3.2). Resistors do not add poles.
Two capacitors in parallel combine into \(C_{1}+C_{2}\) (one independent state) and give only one pole; so can a capacitor loop or a capacitor in series with another one, depending on the connection. So 'at most 2', not always 2.
RC circuits have poles without any inductor.

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit with \(R=50\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=25\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) has output across C: \(H(s)=1/(1+sRC+s^{2}LC)\). Its poles are real. What is the magnitude, in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), of the HIGHER-frequency pole?
questions.explanation:
Poles satisfy \(s^{2}LC+sRC+1=0\), i.e., \(s^{2}+(R/L)s+1/(LC)=0\), with \(R/L=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(1/(LC)=4\times 10^{6}\ s^{-2}\).
\(s=[-5000\pm\sqrt{5000^{2}-4\times 4\times 10^{6}}]/2=[-5000\pm\sqrt{9\times 10^{6}}]/2=(-5000\pm 3000)/2\to s=-1000\) and \(-4000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
The higher pole has magnitude \(4000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Notice neither pole equals \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) or \(R/L=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\): the poles split around \(\omega_{0}\) (their geometric mean is \(\omega_{0}\): \(\sqrt{1000\times 4000}=2000\)).
Common mistake: using \(\omega_{0}=2000\) for both poles.

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit with \(\omega_{0}=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(Q=5\) has a response containing \(e^{st}\) with \(s=-\omega_{0}/(2Q)+j\omega_{0}\sqrt{1-1/(4Q^{2})}=-100+j995\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Compared with its value at \(t=0\) (where \(|e^{st}|=1\)), what is \(|e^{st}|\) at \(t=20\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
Write \(e^{st}=e^{-100t}\cdot e^{j995t}\). The second factor has magnitude 1 (it just rotates), so only the real part of s sets the decay: \(|e^{st}|=e^{-100t}\).
At \(t=20\ \mathrm{ms}\): \(e^{-100\times 0.02}=e^{-2}=0.1353\).
The oscillation frequency \(995\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) does not change the magnitude. Common mistake: including 995 in the exponent, or saying the magnitude stays 1.

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. A later skill writes the poles of the series RLC as \(s=-\omega_{0}/(2Q)\pm j\omega_{0}\sqrt{1-1/(4Q^{2})}\), where \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(Q=(1/R)\sqrt{L/C}\). For \(R=10\ \Omega\), \(L=1\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), what is the decay rate \(\alpha=-\mathrm{Re}\{s\}\) (in \(s^{-1}\)) of the circuit's natural response?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{10^{-9}}=3.162e+04\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). \(Q=(1/10)\sqrt{10^{-3}/10^{-6}}=(1/10)\sqrt{1000}=3.162\).
\(\alpha=\omega_{0}/(2Q)=3.162e+04/(2\times 3.162)=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) (which also equals \(R/(2L)=10/(2\times 10^{-3})=5000\)).
The natural response decays as \(e^{-5000t}\) while oscillating at \(\omega_{0}\sqrt{1-1/(4Q^{2})}\approx 31{,}225\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Common mistake: using \(\omega_{0}/Q=10{,}000\) (the full bandwidth, twice \(\alpha\)).

questions.prompt: Preview of gain-bandwidth. A later skill finds the bandwidth of a feedback amplifier from the op-amp's open-loop Bode plot. An op-amp has \(A(jf)=10^{5}/(1+jf/10\ \mathrm{Hz})\). Using the Bode plot (\(-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) above the 10 Hz pole), at what frequency does |A| fall to 10 (20 dB), the closed-loop gain you want?
questions.explanation:
DC gain \(=10^{5}=100\ \mathrm{dB}\). From the 10 Hz pole, the gain falls \(20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\). To go from 100 dB to 20 dB you need \(80\ \mathrm{dB}=4\) decades: \(10\ \mathrm{Hz}\times 10^{4}=10^{5}\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
Exact: \(|A|=10\) ⇒ \(\sqrt{1+(f/10)^{2}}=10^{4}\) ⇒ \(f=100000\ \mathrm{Hz}\approx 100\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Note that gain \(\times\) frequency stays constant \((10^{5}\times 10\ \mathrm{Hz}=10\times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Hz}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{Hz})\): the 'gain-bandwidth product' of 1 MHz. Common mistake: counting only \(80\ \mathrm{dB}/20=4\) but multiplying by 4 instead of \(10^{4}\).

questions.prompt: Preview of coupling capacitors and frequency response. An AC-coupled amplifier has \(H(jf)=-20\cdot[jf/(20\ \mathrm{Hz})]/[1+jf/(20\ \mathrm{Hz})]\cdot 1/[1+jf/(200\ \mathrm{kHz})]\). What is |H| in dB at \(f=20\ \mathrm{Hz}\) (the low corner)? (The 200 kHz pole is so far away that it contributes almost nothing.)
questions.explanation:
Mid-band gain: \(20\cdot\log_{10}(20)=26.02\ \mathrm{dB}\). At the low corner \(f=20\ \mathrm{Hz}\), the high-pass factor \(jf/f_{L}/(1+jf/f_{L})=j/(1+j)\) has magnitude 0.7071 (−3.01 dB). The 200 kHz pole's factor is \(1/\sqrt{1+10^{-8}}\approx 1\).
\(|H|=20\times 0.7071=14.14\to 23.01\ \mathrm{dB}\ (26.02-3.01)\).
Common mistake: reading the mid-band 26 dB as the gain at the corner; the corner is by definition 3 dB below mid-band.
questions.figure_alt: Band-pass shaped Bode magnitude: rising to 26 dB at 20 Hz, flat, then falling beyond 200 kHz.
